title: The Priest Who Surrendered: Jerusalem, Jotapata, and Twenty Books Written in Rome
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Priest's Son in the Upper City

stops.name: Jerusalem, the priestly quarter: born in the first year of Caligula
stops.date_confidence: attested by his own account, Life 1-6, which dates the birth to the first year of Gaius Caesar, that is 37 or 38 CE. Month and day are unrecorded and defaulted to January 1. The Hasmonaean descent claimed through his mother is self-report only; no registry survives to test it.
stops.campa: A son is born to the priest Matthias in the first year of Gaius Caesar, in the quarter where the priestly houses stand within sight of the sanctuary. The father belongs to Jehoiarib, first of the twenty-four courses that serve the altar in rotation, and the boy is entered on the public registers that keep such descent. He is named Yosef ben Mattityahu. His mother, he will write, carried the blood of the Hasmonaean kings, who were priests as well. Those registers burned with the city thirty-three years later, and no archive survives to confirm the claim or to deny it.
stops.quote: I am not only sprung from a sacerdotal family in general; but from the first of the twenty four courses.
suggested_refs: The priestly registers of Jerusalem, cited by Josephus as public record and destroyed with the city in 70 CE

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Temple: the boy questioned at fourteen
stops.date_confidence: self-report only, Life 9, and a commonplace of the ancient Life genre; nothing outside Josephus records it. Year derived from his stated age of about fourteen. Month and day unrecorded, defaulted.
stops.campa: At fourteen he is already known in the city for his appetite at the page, and the high priests and the principal men come to him, he says, to hear what he thinks about the exact understanding of points of the law. Those are the men who run the Temple courts. He is a boy living in his father's house on the other side of the valley from them. It is the kind of story a man tells about himself when he needs his readers to grant him standing before he asks them to believe anything harder. Nobody else records it.
stops.quote: I was commended by all for the love I had to learning; on which account the High Priests, and principal men of the city came then frequently to me together, in order to know my opinion about the accurate understanding of points of the law.
suggested_refs: The Herodian Temple platform, whose dimensions Josephus later describes at length in Jewish War 5

stops.name: Jerusalem, the three schools weighed
stops.date_confidence: attested in Life 10-11, from his stated age of about sixteen. The chronology of Life 10-12 is internally compressed: three years with Bannus plus a survey of three sects does not fit cleanly between sixteen and nineteen. The compression is his own and is left standing.
stops.campa: At sixteen he sets out to test the sects by living inside them rather than reading about them. A young priest who means to speak for the law wants to be able to say he stood inside every version of it first. He goes to the Pharisees, who hold to the tradition of the fathers; to the Sadducees, drawn from priestly houses like his own; to the Essenes, with their common purse and their washings. He goes through all three, he says, and takes hard labour in each. The years he allows himself for it will not hold everything he says he did in them.
stops.quote: The first is that of the Pharisees, the second that of the Sadducees, and the third that of the Essenes.
suggested_refs: Josephus's parallel account of the three sects at Antiquities 18.11-25, written some forty years later

stops.name: The Judaean wilderness, three years with Bannus
stops.date_confidence: attested in Life 11-12 as an episode of about three years, but the place is never named. The pin follows the conventional scholarly placement in the dry country falling toward the Dead Sea and is inference, not text. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He hears of a man called Bannus living out in the desert and goes to him. Bannus wears what the trees give, eats what grows without planting, and washes himself in cold water by day and by night for purity. Josephus stays three years, imitating him. Of everything he later claims about his youth, this is the part that cost him something to have done. The text names no place, so the desert here is the conventional one, the dry country falling east toward the salt sea, and the hut or cave is nowhere at all. He is nineteen when he comes back.
stops.quote: when I was informed that one, whose name was Banus, lived in the desert...I imitated him...and continued with him three years
stops.quote_source: Josephus, Life 11, Whiston translation (ellipses as rendered by the retrieval tool, not verified as a continuous line)
suggested_refs: The ascetic and baptising movements of first-century Judaea, of which Bannus is the only named individual outside the sectarian literature

stops.name: Jerusalem, nineteen and the rule of the Pharisees
stops.date_confidence: attested in Life 12 at his stated age of nineteen. Whether he lived as a Pharisee or claimed it retrospectively in Rome, once the Pharisaic party had become the surviving one, is a standing scholarly dispute and is not adjudicated here. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He comes back into the city at nineteen and begins to conduct himself by the rules of the Pharisees, a school he later compares, for his Greek readers, to the Stoics. It is an odd choice for a man of the priestly aristocracy, whose kin lean Sadducee, and scholars have argued for a century over whether he really lived that way or only said so once, in Rome, when it had become the useful thing to have been. He offers no explanation. The autobiography moves straight on to his twenty-sixth year.
stops.quote: I returned back to the city, being now nineteen years old, and began to conduct myself according to the rules of the sect of the Pharisees
suggested_refs: The comparison of the Jewish schools to Greek philosophical sects, a device Josephus uses in both Life and Antiquities for a Roman readership

stops.name: The Adriatic, six hundred in the water
stops.date_confidence: attested in Life 13-15 at his stated age of twenty-six, giving 63 or 64 CE. The wreck site is never recorded; the pin is a mid-sea approximation with no textual warrant beyond the word Adriatic. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He sails for Rome at twenty-six to plead for certain priests, good and honest men, whom the procurator Felix has shipped to Nero in chains on a small and trivial charge. The ship goes down in the middle of the Adriatic. Six hundred souls swim the whole night; at first light a Cyrenian vessel comes up and takes eighty of them out of the water. The other five hundred and twenty are not named here or anywhere else in his books. He is one of the eighty, and he calls it the providence of God.
stops.quote: our ship was drowned in the Adriatic Sea...I and some others, eighty in all, by God's providence, prevented the rest
stops.quote_source: Josephus, Life 15, Whiston translation (ellipsis as rendered by the retrieval tool)
suggested_refs: The winter sailing season on the Rome run, closed by law and crossed anyway by embassies in a hurry

stops.name: Puteoli, ashore with the actor Aliturus
stops.date_confidence: attested in Life 16. The pin is the conventional Pozzuoli anchorage. The exact year turns on his stated age of twenty-six and is given variously as 63 or 64 CE; month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Landed at Dicaearchia, which the Italians call Puteoli, he falls in with Aliturus, a comic actor much loved by Nero and a Jew by birth. The port is the empire's front door, where the Alexandrian grain fleet unloads and where anyone with business at the palace comes ashore. What the errand needs is access, and a man who can make Caesar laugh has it. Josephus is twenty-six and has been in Italy a matter of days. The introduction that will decide the errand is made here on the bay, a hundred and fifty miles short of Rome.
stops.quote: when I was in the twenty-sixth year of my age, it happened that I took a voyage to Rome
suggested_refs: The harbour mole at Puteoli, principal landing for eastern traffic before Ostia was enlarged

stops.name: Rome, the Palatine: Poppaea and the priests released
stops.date_confidence: attested in Life 16 as to the introduction, the intercession, and the gifts. Josephus names no building in Rome; the Palatine pin is inference from where the imperial household then was. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Aliturus brings him to Poppaea Sabina, the emperor's wife, who is well disposed toward Jewish causes, and through her the imprisoned priests are set free. Nothing in the episode belongs to the register of prophecy or providence: a young man from a subject province is introduced to the right woman by the right actor, and it works. He has also seen the machine from the inside, the size of the army and the temper of the court, and he will spend the next two years telling his countrymen that this is not a thing they can fight. He leaves with gifts from Poppaea besides, and sails home.
suggested_refs: Poppaea Sabina's documented interventions on behalf of Jewish petitioners, also reported at Antiquities 20.195

stops.name: Jerusalem, home to a city already arming
stops.date_confidence: attested as narrative in Life 17-19, but every statement of his own motive here is self-report written after 71 CE, in Rome, on a Flavian pension. Treat the sequence of events as attested and the intention behind it as untestable. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He returns to find the revolutionary party already moving, and by his own account he tries to hold it back, telling them plainly that they are inferior to the Romans in war and had better not risk it. They take him for a collaborator. He withdraws into the inner court of the Temple for safety and waits there until the Roman commander Metilius is dead and the thing is past mending. Every word of this account is his, written thirty years afterward, in the capital of the people who won. It may still be exactly what happened.
suggested_refs: The massacre of the Roman garrison under Metilius, Jewish War 2.450-456, the point after which no negotiated settlement remained available

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Temple: commissioned after Beth Horon
stops.date_confidence: attested, but with a contradiction between his own two accounts that is flagged and not resolved: Jewish War 2.562-568 makes him general of Galilee with plenary charge, while Life 28-29 makes him one of three priests sent to pacify the province. Autumn 66 is secure from the Beth Horon date; day defaulted.
stops.campa: Cestius Gallus marches on Jerusalem, hesitates before the walls, withdraws, and is cut to pieces in the pass at Beth Horon. The province understands that Rome will come back in earnest. The authorities in the Temple divide the country into commands and send Josephus north into Galilee. In the War he goes as a general with charge of the whole region. In the Life, written thirty years later against a man who was there, he goes as one of three priests sent to calm the province and disarm the hotheads. Both accounts are his.
suggested_refs: The Beth Horon pass, where the Twelfth Legion lost its eagle in autumn 66

stops.name: Sepphoris, the largest city will not come
stops.date_confidence: attested in Life 30 and 373-380 and Jewish War 2.574; the site identification at Tzippori is secure from excavation. The month is not fixed by any source and is defaulted to the winter of 66/67 by narrative position.
stops.campa: Sepphoris sits on its hill above the plain, the largest city in Galilee, minted and administered and comfortable, and it has no intention of dying for Jerusalem. Josephus takes the town, loses it, negotiates with it, and is nearly killed by it, over and over through the winter. In Galilee the war he was sent to organise is largely a war among Galileans over whether there should be a war at all. Sepphoris will open its gates to Vespasian without a fight and take a Roman garrison inside its walls.
suggested_refs: Sepphoris coins of the revolt years struck with Vespasian's name and the legend Eirenopolis, city of peace
sources: Israel Antiquities Authority excavations, Tzippori National Park

stops.name: Tiberias, the walls and the threatened hand
stops.date_confidence: attested as self-report in Life 96-100 and 168-173. There is no independent record of the episode, and the man who could have supplied one, Justus of Tiberias, wrote a history that is lost. Month defaulted by narrative position.
stops.campa: Herod Antipas built this city on the lake and named it for a Caesar; Josephus walls it. He also, by his own telling, faces down a hostile assembly here by having a man seized and threatening to strike off his hand, at which the crowd scatters. He records the trick without embarrassment, along with several others, as evidence of the resourcefulness a command required. Justus of Tiberias was in the city through all of it and wrote his own version. It is lost, and the only summary of it comes from Photius, eight centuries later.
suggested_refs: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 33, the sole surviving notice of Justus of Tiberias and his history
sources: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 33 (cited at second hand)

stops.name: Tarichaeae, the execution that is not one
stops.date_confidence: attested as self-report in Life 138-144. The site is identified with excavated Magdala on the lake shore. The episode has no independent witness. Month defaulted by narrative position within the Galilean command.
stops.campa: At Tarichaeae on the lake shore, where the fishing town salts its catch for the whole province, he suspects mutiny and stages a punishment. He tells the story on himself, inside a book whose whole purpose is to show that he governed Galilee well, and offers it there as evidence that he did. A man is thrown down. A guard stands over him with a drawn sword and the assembly watches. The blade does not fall; the man gets up unharmed, and the mutiny does not happen.
suggested_refs: The excavated harbour, synagogue and fish-salting installations of Magdala on the western shore of the lake

stops.name: Gischala, John and the other account
stops.date_confidence: attested in Life 43-45 and 70-76, but the portrait is uniformly hostile and largely uncheckable in its particulars. Coordinates corrected to the village of Jish, 33.0261 35.4453; the value in the research pool sat about 1.4 km south of the site. Day set to order the segment.
stops.campa: John son of Levi holds Gischala in the upper hills, and across the pages of the War and the Life he is Josephus's opposite in every particular: greedy, treacherous, a cornerer of the olive oil market, a man who wanted the Galilean command for himself. Everything anyone knows about him was written by the man he tried to have removed. What he thought of Josephus is recorded nowhere. He will end the war leading a faction inside besieged Jerusalem, and be carried through Rome in the triumph and sentenced to prison for life.
suggested_refs: John of Gischala's later career in the factional war inside Jerusalem, Jewish War 4-6
sources: Josephus, Jewish War 6.433 (John's surrender and sentence of perpetual imprisonment)

stops.name: Gamla, the camel's back fortified
stops.date_confidence: attested in Life 187 as one of his fortifications and narrated at length in Jewish War 4.4-83. Whether the works were his order or the townsmen's own is not resolvable. The archaeology is secure. Day set to order the segment.
stops.campa: On a ridge shaped like a camel above the Golan ravines, Gamla is walled at his order, or so he says; the townsmen may well have done it themselves. Vespasian will take it in the autumn after a first assault collapses in the narrow streets and kills his own men. Unlike most of the Galilean material in his books, this place answers back. Excavation has turned up the wall, the ballista stones by the hundred, the arrowheads in the burnt layer, and coins struck in the town during the revolt.
suggested_refs: The Israel Antiquities Authority excavations at Gamla: the breached wall, the ballista stones, the coins of the revolt struck in the town
sources: Israel Antiquities Authority excavations at Gamla

stops.name: Mount Tabor, the summit walled in forty days
stops.date_confidence: attested in Life 188 as one of the fortified points and in Jewish War 4.54-61 for its fall. The forty-day figure is Josephus's own and has no external check. Day set to order the segment.
stops.campa: The mountain stands alone off the plain of Esdraelon, round and steep, with a level top wide enough to hold a town. Josephus lists it among the places he fortified, and says the wall around its summit went up in forty days, with every jar of water and every stone carried up from below. The Galilee he is preparing is a chain of hilltops, each meant to hold alone: the plan of a man who does not expect to win a battle in open country. In the summer Placidus lures the defenders down onto that plain and takes the height from them without a siege.
suggested_refs: The summit plateau of Tabor and its later Byzantine and Crusader building, which overlies whatever the 67 CE wall was

stops.name: The caves of Arbela, a cliff refortified
stops.date_confidence: attested in Life 188. The pin follows the cliffs of Mount Arbel above the pass west of the lake. The Herodian siege recalled in the campa is at Antiquities 14.415-430, a separate and much earlier event. Day set to order the segment.
stops.campa: Above the pass where the road from the lake climbs west, the cliff of Arbel is riddled with caves in its face, reachable only by ropes let down from the top. Herod took them a hundred years earlier by lowering cages of soldiers on chains with grappling hooks and burning the rebels out of the rock. Josephus names the caves in his list of works. He is fortifying a place whose most famous story is how it fell, and he is the man who tells that story, at length, with the old man in the cave killing his own children rather than surrender.
suggested_refs: Josephus, Antiquities 14.415-430, his own account of Herod's assault on the same caves

stops.name: The rock of Acchabaron, above the gorge
stops.date_confidence: attested in Life 187 as a name on the fortification list; the identification with Akbara south of Safed is conventional rather than certain. Coordinates corrected to 32.9394, 35.4994; the research pool's value lay about 5.7 km too far north, placing the site north of Safed instead of south of it. Day set to order the segment.
stops.campa: Among the strongholds of the upper country he names the rock of Acchabaron. The village below it, in the gorge south of Safed, keeps the name still; the fortified thing itself is the cliff and its caves rather than the houses. In the Life these places arrive in a plain list, one after another with no incident attached to any of them, a quartermaster's inventory and not a story. He sets the names down because the list itself is the proof that the work was done. Several of them have never been securely matched to any ground.
suggested_refs: The cliff caves south of Akbara and the ruin at Khirbet al-Uqeiba, the two candidates for Josephus's rock of Acchabaron

stops.name: Meroth, the far edge of the command
stops.date_confidence: attested in Life 187 as a name on the list and nowhere else in his works. Identification with the excavated site of Merot is scholarly consensus, not certainty. Coordinates corrected to 33.0286, 35.5283, some 7 km northeast of Safed; the pool's value sat almost on top of its own mistaken Gischala pin. Day set to order the segment.
stops.campa: Meroth lies northeast of Safed in the high country, at the far edge of the ground he was sent to hold. It appears once, in the list of fortifications, and then never again. Whether the walls he claims were ever built there, or built by him, cannot be tested, and the identification of the site itself is agreement rather than proof. By late spring the Romans are across the frontier with three legions and their auxiliaries, and the whole scheme of walled hilltops will be settled in a matter of weeks.
suggested_refs: The excavated village and synagogue at Merot in the Upper Galilee, the conventional identification of Josephus's Meroth

stops.name: Japha, the town beside Nazareth
stops.date_confidence: attested in Life 188 as a fortification and in Jewish War 3.289-306 for its destruction. Josephus is not present at the storming; the casualty figures are his and cannot be checked against anything. Day approximated to the Roman advance of early summer 67.
stops.campa: Japha sits in the folds below the ridge of Nazareth, a large village behind a double wall, and it is on his list. In the summer it will be stormed by Trajan the elder and then by Titus, and the two walls will trap its own people between them. Josephus counts fifteen thousand dead there and two thousand one hundred and thirty women and children taken. He gives the numbers as he gives all his numbers, precisely and with no means of checking them. He is not there. He is ten miles west, inside Jotapata, watching the dust of the column that is coming for him.
suggested_refs: Yafa an-Naseriyye, the modern town on the site of Japha, immediately southwest of Nazareth

stops.name: Jotapata, forty-seven days on the precipice
stops.date_confidence: attested in Jewish War 3.141-339 and materially corroborated by the Yodefat excavations of 1992-2000 under Mordechai Aviam: fortifications, cisterns, siege debris, weapon-trauma remains, a mass grave. Coordinates corrected to the ancient tell at 32.8319, 35.2781, per Wikidata Q1517688; the pool's value lay 4.4 km northwest on open hillside. Day defaulted.
stops.campa: The town stands on a spur cut off on three sides by ravines so deep that the eye fails looking down into them. Vespasian brings two legions against it in May. The Romans raise a bank; the defenders raise the wall higher behind screens of raw hides. The rams beat; the townsmen pour boiling oil that runs inside the armour and scalds men to the bone. When the water runs low Josephus has the last of it poured down the outside of the wall in full view, so the besiegers will believe there is plenty. Forty-seven days. Then a deserter tells them the dawn watch sleeps, and they come over in the fog.
suggested_refs: The Yodefat excavations, six seasons 1992-2000, Mordechai Aviam for the Israel Antiquities Authority and the University of Rochester

stops.name: Jotapata, the cistern and the lot
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Jewish War 3.340-391 is the sole witness to this episode and nothing outside Josephus's own narrative attests the cave, the pact, the lot, or its outcome. The research pool's two lenses disagreed, one tagging it attested and one reconstruction; the stricter tag is adopted here. The 20 July date is the traditional one for the fall of the town.
stops.campa: Forty of the leading men are hidden with him in a cave off a cistern. On the third day a woman gives the place away. The Romans call up and offer his life; the others will not have it and turn their swords toward him, and he proposes instead that they kill one another in an order drawn by lot, each man taking the throat of the one before him. He is left standing with one other man. He talks that man into surrender. The arithmetic of the lot has been picked over ever since. Nothing outside his own pages attests the cave, the pact, the lot, or the outcome.
stops.quote: Since it pleaseth thee, who hast created the Jewish nation, to depress the same, and since all their good fortune is gone over to the Romans, and since thou hast made choice of this soul of mine to foretel what is to come to pass hereafter, I willingly give them my hands, and am content to live.
suggested_refs: The mathematical literature on the Josephus problem, an elimination puzzle named for a scene attested by one man about himself

stops.name: Jotapata, the Roman camp: the prophecy
stops.date_confidence: attested in Jewish War 3.392-408 and, unusually for this life, corroborated externally: Suetonius, Vespasian 5, and Cassius Dio 66.1.4. The two versions differ. Dio has Josephus name a one-year deadline, which appears nowhere in Josephus; Josephus includes Titus in the prophecy, which Dio does not. Day set to follow the surrender.
stops.campa: Brought bound before Vespasian, he asks to speak apart and tells the general that he is not a captive but a messenger, and that Vespasian will be Caesar, and his son after him. Vespasian is fifty-eight, of no distinguished family, and serving an emperor who is alive in Rome. He keeps the prisoner and does not send him on to Nero. Two years later, at Alexandria, it comes true. Suetonius and Dio both carry the story a century afterward, and Dio adds a deadline of one year that Josephus himself never wrote.
stops.quote: Thou, O Vespasian, art Caesar and emperor, thou, and this thy son.
suggested_refs: Tacitus, Histories 5.13, on the eastern oracle that a ruler of the world would come out of Judaea

stops.name: Caesarea Maritima, kept and not sent to Nero
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the two years of custody, Jewish War 3.408 and Life 414. Josephus does not itemise where he was held; Caesarea is the conventional inference from its being Vespasian's provincial headquarters. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Vespasian's headquarters are in the Herodian port, with its harbour and hippodrome and aqueduct, the administrative capital of a province in revolt. Josephus is held there some two years, in chains but well used, given clothing and other precious gifts. The prophecy is his security. So long as it has not been disproved he is worth keeping alive, and so long as it has not been fulfilled he is worth keeping quiet. The war goes on to the north of him and to the south of him and he takes no part in either.
suggested_refs: Caesarea Maritima, the Roman provincial capital of Judaea, and its excavated harbour works

stops.name: Caesarea Maritima, married among the captives
stops.date_confidence: attested as self-report in Life 414: the marriage is arranged during his captivity, at Vespasian's direction, to one of the captive women, and she leaves him when he is freed. She is unnamed and undated in the text. Year and day are set by narrative position within the captivity.
stops.campa: While he is still a prisoner Vespasian orders him to marry, and the woman is one of the captives taken at Caesarea. He records the arrangement in a single clause of his autobiography, without her name, and adds that she did not stay with him once he was freed. Three marriages appear in that book and all three are disposed of at about that speed. He will later give twenty books to other people's houses, their descents and their quarrels, at a length no woman of his own gets. His mother, held inside Jerusalem through the siege, has one sentence.
suggested_refs: Life 414-427, the whole of Josephus's account of his three marriages and five children, running to under a page

stops.name: Alexandria, the chains cut with an axe
stops.date_confidence: attested in Jewish War 4.622-629 for the release and the axe, and in Life 414-415 for the Alexandrian marriage, which the text places at Alexandria after the release and before the siege of Jerusalem. This corrects the research pool's chronology lens, which placed the marriage at Rome in 71. Day defaulted to the proclamation month.
stops.campa: In July the eastern legions proclaim Vespasian emperor and the prisoner becomes a prophet. Titus advises that his chains be not simply unlocked but cut through with an axe, so that the fact of his having been bound is annulled and no mark of it remains on him. Freed at Alexandria, Josephus marries there, a Jewish woman of that city. Then Titus turns south for Judaea and Josephus goes with him, on the other side of the war he was sent north to fight. Three sons come of the Alexandrian marriage. Two die small; Hyrcanus lives.
suggested_refs: Jewish War 4.622-629, where the axe rather than the key is Titus's own suggestion

stops.name: Mount Scopus, the camp above the city
stops.date_confidence: attested in Jewish War 5.67-70 and 5.261 for the camp positions and his presence with the army. The siege opens around Passover of 70; the exact day of his arrival is not recorded and is defaulted.
stops.campa: The legions pitch on the shoulder north of the city, and from that ridge the whole of it lies open: the third wall, the fortress of Antonia, the great platform with the sanctuary white and gold at the top of it. He is thirty-three, a freedman in Roman pay, looking down at the courts where high priests once came to ask his opinion. His work now is language. He interprets deserters, reads the mood inside the walls for Titus, and carries terms across. The siege begins at Passover, with the city full of pilgrims who cannot get out.
suggested_refs: The camp positions of the Fifth, Twelfth and Fifteenth legions before Jerusalem, Jewish War 5.67-70

stops.name: Jerusalem, below the wall: struck by a stone
stops.date_confidence: attested as self-report in Jewish War 5.361-420 and 5.541-547. No Roman record confirms the wounding or the speeches. Month approximated from the narrative sequence of the siege; day defaulted.
stops.campa: He goes round the circuit of the wall calling up to the defenders in Hebrew, as one of them, arguing that God has gone over to the Romans and that the city can still be spared if they open the gates. The men on the wall call him a traitor and shoot down at him. A stone catches him on the head and he drops; the Romans carry him off and the rumour of his death runs through the city and briefly cheers it. He recovers, and goes back the next day to stand under the same wall and say the same thing.
suggested_refs: The surrender speeches of Jewish War 5.362-419, the longest sustained argument Josephus puts in his own mouth

stops.name: Jerusalem, inside the wall: his father in prison
stops.date_confidence: attested at Jewish War 5.544-545, where the captors are called only 'the seditious' and no faction is named. This corrects the research pool, which attributed the detention to Simon bar Giora and cited 5.533; that passage is the murder of a different Matthias, the high priest, son of Boethus. Month approximated; day defaulted.
stops.campa: His father is shut up in prison by the rebels and his mother is put under guard, and the report of it reaches him outside the wall. In the same book, a few paragraphs off, the faction leader Simon kills another Matthias, a high priest who had opened a gate to him, together with three of his sons. Two men of that name lie close enough in the text to be mistaken for each other, and exactly one of them is his father. He says his mother asked, whenever she was let to speak, whether her son was still alive.
suggested_refs: Jewish War 5.527-533, the killing of Matthias son of Boethus by Simon bar Giora, routinely conflated with the imprisonment of Josephus's own father

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Temple courts: the sanctuary burns
stops.date_confidence: attested in Jewish War 6.220-270 and dated by Josephus to the tenth of the month Lous, conventionally rendered late August or early September 70. The question of who ordered the fire is contested: Sulpicius Severus, Chronica 2.30.6-7, probably drawing on the lost books of Tacitus, holds that Titus argued for destruction. Flagged, not resolved.
stops.campa: Fire takes the sanctuary. Josephus writes that Titus called a council, said he wished the building spared, and was pre-empted by a soldier who, moved by a divine impulse and ordered by nobody, snatched a brand and threw it through a golden window. He is writing as the client of that same Titus. Three centuries later Sulpicius Severus preserves the opposite account, probably out of the lost books of Tacitus: that Titus argued for the destruction, to pull up the religion by its root. Those two accounts are the whole of the evidence.
stops.quote_source: Josephus, Jewish War 6.299-300, reporting the voice the priests said they heard in the Temple at Pentecost before the war
suggested_refs: Sulpicius Severus, Chronica 2.30.6-7, the rival tradition on the burning of the Temple
sources: Sulpicius Severus, Chronica 2.30.6-7 (cited at second hand)

stops.name: Jerusalem, the ruined city: the brother, the friends, the books
stops.date_confidence: attested as self-report in Life 418-419 and Jewish War 6.428 for the sacred books. The fate of his mother after the siege is never stated anywhere in his works; his father's release is likewise unreported. Day approximated to the weeks after the fall.
stops.campa: With the city taken he asks Titus for things and is given them: his brother Matthias out of the captives, then some fifty friends, then a hundred and ninety more found among the women and children penned in the Temple court. He asks for the sacred books out of the plunder and gets those too, and walks out of the ruin with his brother, his friends and the scrolls. Sent later on an errand, he passes a road of the crucified and recognises three of them, and Titus has all three taken down and given to the physicians. Two die under their hands. The third lives.
suggested_refs: Life 418-421, the requests granted to Josephus by Titus after the fall, including the three men taken down from their crosses

stops.name: Rome, the Sacred Way: the triumph of the spoils
stops.date_confidence: attested in Jewish War 7.116-157, and Josephus's presence in Rome with Titus in Life 422-423. The exact date of the triumph within 71 CE is not fixed by the sources; month and day are approximate. The Arch of Titus, which carves the same procession, was dedicated after 81 and postdates his presence at the event.
stops.campa: Vespasian and Titus celebrate the Judaean triumph together, and the procession comes down the Sacred Way with the spoils of the Temple carried openly: the golden table, the lampstand with its seven branches, and last of all the Law of the Jews. Josephus watches from inside the emperor's household, a free man, and writes the fullest account of the day that anyone has. Simon son of Gioras is dragged along at the end of it with a rope round his neck and killed in the Forum. Word is brought up that it has been done, and the sacrifices begin.
suggested_refs: The Arch of Titus relief on the Via Sacra, showing the menorah and the table carried in this procession

stops.name: Rome, a house that had been Vespasian's
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to place. Life 423 says only that Vespasian gave him lodging in the house he had lived in before he came to the empire; Josephus never names a district. The Quirinal placement rests on Suetonius's separate note that the Flavian family house stood in Region VI, ad Malum Punicum. Citizenship, pension and land are attested at Life 423 and Against Apion 1.51-52. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Vespasian gives him lodging in the house he himself lived in before he came to the empire, along with Roman citizenship, a pension, and land in Judaea to replace what the war took. The address is nowhere stated. Suetonius puts the Flavian family house in the sixth region, at the pomegranate tree, and the district here follows that inference and not any word of Josephus's own. He takes the family name of his patrons at about this time, and from here on the books go out under it. Yosef ben Mattityahu of the course of Jehoiarib is now Flavius Josephus of Rome.
suggested_refs: Suetonius on the Flavian house ad Malum Punicum in Region VI, later the site of the Templum Gentis Flaviae

stops.name: Rome, the Temple of Peace: where the vessels are put
stops.date_confidence: attested that Josephus describes the precinct and the deposit of the Temple vessels, Jewish War 7.158-162, and the Temple of Peace was dedicated in 75. Whether he ever entered it is not stated anywhere and should not be assumed; the stop is for his account of it. Month and day defaulted to the dedication year.
stops.campa: Vespasian raises a precinct to Peace out of the Judaean money and fills it with the masterpieces of the world, and into it go the golden vessels out of Jerusalem. The Law and the purple curtains he keeps in the palace instead. Josephus sets the arrangement down himself, in the last book of the War, plainly and without complaint, a man noting where the furniture of his father's house has been put. Whether he ever went in to look at it, across twenty-five years of living a mile away, he does not say.
suggested_refs: The Templum Pacis precinct and the deposition of the Temple vessels described at Jewish War 7.158-162

stops.name: Rome, the seven books presented
stops.date_confidence: attested in Jewish War 1.3-6, Life 361-363 and Against Apion 1.50-51. The completion is placed between 75 and 79 by the dedication to Vespasian and Titus; no closer date is recoverable. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He finishes the War in Greek, seven books, using assistants for the language, and puts copies into the hands of Vespasian and of Titus, who signs an order that they be published. An earlier version had gone east first, written in his own tongue for the Parthians and the Babylonians and the Jews beyond the Euphrates. The book that told the story in Aramaic to the people it happened to is the one that was lost. Not one line of it survives, and no ancient writer quotes it. What survives is the Greek, made in the capital, for the readers of the people who won.
suggested_refs: The lost Aramaic first edition of Jewish War, announced by Josephus at War 1.3 and unattested in any fragment or quotation

stops.name: Rome, the letters of Agrippa
stops.date_confidence: attested as self-report quoting a lost original: Life 364-367, where Josephus says Agrippa II wrote him sixty-two letters and quotes two. No original survives, and nothing whatever of Agrippa II survives outside Josephus. Year approximate; month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He sends the finished books to King Agrippa the Second, last of the Herods, who spent the war on the Roman side and knows the ground as well as any man living. Agrippa writes back sixty-two letters, Josephus says, and the two he sets out call the work accurate and invite him to come and be told the rest. The witness and the man who vouches for the witness reach the modern world bound into the same volume. The originals do not survive. Nothing at all of Agrippa survives outside these books.
suggested_refs: Life 364-367, the two quoted letters of Agrippa II, the only words of that king anyone has

stops.name: Rome, Domitian's court: the accusers punished
stops.date_confidence: attested as self-report, Life 428-429, and it is the sole record: no tribunal document, no external notice, and no statement of what the accusations were. Titus reigned 79 to 81 and Domitian 81 to 96; the year here is set mid-reign to order the segment. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Titus dies after two years and his brother takes the empire, and the pension holds. Josephus reports that Domitian punished the Jews who accused him, exempted his Judaean land from tax, and that Domitia, the emperor's wife, never stopped doing him kindnesses. The reign that kills senators for a sentence leaves the Jewish historian alone in his house with his twenty books. He was accused more than once, and by his own countrymen. What the accusations said he never tells, and no one else records them.
suggested_refs: Life 428-430, the closing paragraphs on Flavian patronage and the unspecified accusations against him

segments.name: The Twenty Books, and the Silence

stops.name: Rome, the thirteenth year of Domitian
stops.date_confidence: attested by Josephus's own colophon at Antiquities 20.267, the thirteenth year of Domitian and the fifty-sixth of his life, that is 93 or 94 CE. It is the last securely datable statement of any kind about him. The dedicatee Epaphroditus cannot be securely identified. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Twenty books, from the creation of the world down to the outbreak of the war he fought in, dedicated to a patron named Epaphroditus whose identity nobody has ever settled: Nero's freedman secretary, killed by Domitian, or a grammarian of the same name. At the end Josephus dates himself, as a scribe dates a colophon, by the emperor's regnal year and his own age together. He is fifty-six. Everything after this in his biography is inference, and there is not much of it.
stops.quote: the thirteenth year of the reign of Caesar Domitian, and the fifty-sixth year of my own life
suggested_refs: Antiquities 1.8-9 and Life 430, the recurring dedications to Epaphroditus across the later works

stops.name: Rome, from the flood to the house of the Lord
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the contents of Antiquities I to VIII. The four-storey ark is at Antiquities 1.77, the Place of Descent at 1.92, the Tyrian archives behind the Temple account at 8.144-149 and Against Apion 1.106-127. The dates in this segment order the works, not events; the books were written across the preceding decade.
stops.campa: He tells Noah's flood again for Greek readers, giving the ark four storeys where Genesis gives three, and reports that the Armenians of his own day still call the landing place the Place of Descent. Aaron, from whose line his own priesthood runs, comes in the third book; Moses he defends against the Egyptian polemicists as a lawgiver. He tells David and Solomon and the raising of the first Temple out of the Tyrian archives, naming Hiram the king who sent the cedars and the Tyrian craftsman of the same name who cast the bronze pillars, and reporting the murder of no master workman at all.
suggested_refs: Antiquities 8.144-149, where Josephus cites Menander of Ephesus on the correspondence between Tyre and Jerusalem over the Temple

stops.name: Rome, the burning of the first house
stops.date_confidence: attested as to contents of Antiquities X. The notice that Ezekiel left two books is at Antiquities 10.79 and Josephus names no authority for it; no second book has ever been identified. The date orders the segment and is not an event date.
stops.campa: Book Ten carries the kingdom down to its end. Nebuchadnezzar comes up out of Babylon, the Temple burns, the people are carried off. Where the Hebrew record goes quiet Josephus reaches for Greek books that no longer exist, Berossus and the annals of Tyre, and copies out of them whatever will serve. Ezekiel is there among the exiles by the river, and Josephus notes, in passing and on no authority he names, that the prophet left behind two books and not one. Nobody has ever found the second.
suggested_refs: Antiquities 10.79, the notice of Ezekiel's two books, unattested anywhere else in antiquity
sources: Josephus, Against Apion 1.128-160 (Berossus and the Tyrian annals)

stops.name: Rome, the two passages about Jesus
stops.date_confidence: the transmitted text is attested; its authenticity is not. Antiquities 18.63-64 contains confessional Christian phrasing that most modern scholarship regards as at least partly a later insertion, with Eusebius in the fourth century the earliest secure witness to the received wording. Antiquities 20.200 is more widely accepted as authentic, though not universally. Flagged as disputed, resolved in neither direction. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: In the eighteenth book, set between a riot over an aqueduct and a scandal in the temple of Isis, stands a paragraph about a wise man called Jesus, which as the manuscripts have it says flatly that he was the Christ. In the twentieth, at the deposition of the high priest Ananus, stands a second and much quieter mention: James, the brother of Jesus who was called Christ, stoned in the year 62. The first passage has been fought over since Eusebius quoted it in the fourth century. The second is generally let stand.
suggested_refs: Codex Ambrosianus 370 (F 128), Biblioteca Ambrosiana, Milan, the earliest Greek manuscript carrying the Testimonium

stops.name: Rome, the Life written against a dead man's book
stops.date_confidence: the text is attested and transmitted appended to the Antiquities manuscripts. Its date is disputed, ranging from the mid-90s to about 100 CE, the argument turning on when Agrippa II died. Year chosen within that range to order the segment; month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Justus of Tiberias, who was in Galilee when Josephus was, publishes a history of the war and lays the blame for his own city's revolt on the general who had been sent to prevent it. Josephus answers with a book about himself, the greater part of which defends six months in Galilee thirty years gone, argued point by point as though before a court. Justus he calls a liar and worse than a liar. The reply survives entire; the book it answers is gone. Photius, reading Justus in the ninth century, found the history very concise and thought it left out most of what mattered. Nobody since reports having had it in hand.
suggested_refs: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 33, the ninth-century summary that is all that remains of Justus of Tiberias
sources: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 33 (cited at second hand)

stops.name: Rome, Against Apion and the twenty-two books
stops.date_confidence: attested as later than the Antiquities by its own opening sentence, Against Apion 1.1, which refers back to the completed work; the year is a conventional placement in the later 90s and is not fixed by any source. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Two books, written after the Antiquities and against the grammarians of Alexandria who said the Jews were a recent people with no history. He answers them with archives: the Egyptian priest Manetho, the Babylonian Berossus, and Menander of Ephesus, who translated the records of Tyre out of Phoenician. Out of Menander come the letters that passed between Hiram of Tyre and Solomon over the building of the Temple, and the king-list that runs down to the seventh year of Pygmalion, in which Carthage was founded in Libya. It is the only fixed date antiquity has for Dido's city.
stops.quote: we have not an innumerable multitude of books among us, disagreeing from, and contradicting one another: [as the Greeks have:] but only twenty two books
stops.quote_source: Josephus, Against Apion 1.8, Whiston translation, brackets Whiston's own
suggested_refs: Against Apion 1.106-127, the extracts from Menander of Ephesus on the Tyrian king-list and the archives of Tyre

stops.name: Rome, where the record stops
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction throughout. No ancient source states when, where or how Josephus died, or where he was buried, and no grave was ever shown. The conventional c. 100 CE is a modern estimate resting on the absence of later work; the pin is a general Rome placement with no textual warrant. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: After the thirteenth year of Domitian there is nothing. No writer of antiquity says where he died, or when, or how, and no grave was ever shown for him in Rome or in Judaea. The date around the turn of the century printed in the reference books is a modern estimate resting on the assumption that a man who stopped writing had stopped living. There is no face either; the busts and engravings that carry his name are inventions. What there is instead is the corpus, copied for a thousand years by Christian monks on account of one disputed paragraph, and by nobody else at all.
suggested_refs: Tessa Rajak, Josephus: The Historian and His Society, 2nd ed. (Duckworth, 2002)

The Greek editio princeps, Basel, Hieronymus Froben, 1544, edited by Arnoldus Arlenius; Whiston's English of 1737; Niese's Flavii Iosephi Opera, 7 vols., 1885-1895, whose numbering is still the citation standard
sources: Absence of any ancient notice after Antiquities, Life and Against Apion
